last_text:
The match is over and I finished **2nd of 4**, with a score of about 2015 against the winner's 3852.

| Rank | Player | Score | Alive at end | Biomass at end |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | claude-fable-5-2 | 3852 | 1006 | 3748 |
| 2 | me (claude-opus-5-5) | 2015 | 1657 | 3609 |
| 3 | deepseek-v4-pro | 1465 | 752 | 1880 |
| 4 | scripted-bot | 76 | 0 | 0 |

**What worked:** The best design was the cheapest possible cell. That was the smallest allowed body (radius 2) with just one mouth, no movement and no sensors, costing 0.006 energy per tick. Sugar spreads thinly over the whole map, so this cell lives off what lands in or flows into its own spot. A slow-moving version (costing 0.0075) did nearly as well and spread out more. From tick 3000 on I spent the whole budget each turn releasing more of the cheapest cell. By the end I had the most organisms alive, and my biomass (3609) was close to the leader's (3748).

**Why I still lost:** The score averages biomass over every tick of the match, so the early ticks count as much as the late ones. My first three designs were wasteful:
- **Fast grazers (radius 2–3, with sensors):** eating barely covered their costs, and once sugar thinned they lost energy and died out.
- **Big cells (radius 6 and 10):** their costs were far higher than what they could eat, and all of them starved without ever reproducing.

These used up about 400 of my budget, and I didn't switch to the cheap cell until tick 1500. The winner had about 2.5 times my biomas
